extracted.intended_audience: higher education institutions, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and grievance-process administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory guidance and requirements governing how recipients (colleges/universities) must structure and operate Title IX grievance processes for handling formal complaints of sexual harassment, including evidence access, timelines, training, supportive measures, and use of trauma-informed approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative report distribution requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Revised §106.45(b)(5)(vii) requires the investigative report to be sent to the parties and their advisors (if any).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The investigative report must be provided to both parties and any advisors, for the same reasons the Department requires sending evidence subject to inspect and review to the parties and their advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access to evidence / inspection and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence subject to inspection and review must be sent to the parties and their advisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must provide parties (and their advisors, if any) access to evidence used in the investigation so parties can inspect and review materials that will be used in the grievance process; this is tied to fairness, accuracy, and parties' ability to respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation timeframe expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: An adequate investigation into sexual harassment allegations typically takes longer than 20 days; OCR's experience suggests approximately 60 calendar days following receipt of the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes prior guidance (2011 Dear Colleague Letter) and commenters' experience to justify that typical investigations take around 60 days; institutions should not adopt an unduly short 20-day cap as the norm for adequate investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal application of recipient-adopted rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The introductory sentence of §106.45(b) provides that any provisions, rules, or practices other than those required by this section that a recipient adopts as part of its grievance process must apply equally to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are permitted to adopt additional rules for the Title IX grievance process, but must apply those rules equally to both complainant and respondent. This includes procedural rules, evidentiary practices, or rules about advisors or conduct in proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker training on relevance and rape-shield protections
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45(b)(1)(iii) specifically requires that decision-makers are trained on issues of relevance, including application of the “rape shield” protections in §106.45(b)(6).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers must receive training that enables them to assess relevance and apply statutory protections (e.g., rape-shield rules) when evaluating evidence and testimony; this supports fair adjudication and consistent application of protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of treatment records limited to voluntary written consent
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(5)(i) provides that a party's treatment records can only be used in a grievance process with that party's voluntary, written consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions may not require disclosure or use of confidential treatment/medical records without the party's voluntary written approval; protect privacy and comply with this consent requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures: offer and notice requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.44(a) requires recipients to offer supportive measures to a complainant, and the Title IX Coordinator must promptly contact the complainant to discuss availability of supportive measures, inform them of availability with or without filing a formal complaint, and explain the process for filing a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions must proactively offer individualized supportive measures, explain they are available regardless of filing a formal complaint, and document outreach by the Title IX Coordinator so complainants can make informed choices about participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance process must describe supportive measures available
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 defines “supportive measures” and §106.45(b)(1)(ix) requires a recipient's grievance process to describe the range of supportive measures available to complainants and to respondents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published grievance procedures should include a clear description of the types of supportive measures (for both parties) so parties understand options and recipients demonstrate transparency and compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on retaliation and protection of non-participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.71 prohibits retaliation for exercise of rights under Title IX and specifically protects any individual's right to not participate in a grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must have and enforce anti-retaliation protections; individuals must not be coerced into participating and must be protected if they choose not to engage in the grievance process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive but constrained use of trauma-informed approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients have flexibility to employ trauma-informed approaches, but the Department does not mandate them; because there is no singular definition and varied contexts, such approaches must be applied carefully to ensure impartial investigations and compliance with all regulatory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigators should receive trauma-informed training to avoid re-traumatizing complainants during investigation. However, trauma-informed approaches to evaluating testimony must not lead adjudicators to overlook significant inconsistencies; investigators and adjudicators should consider and balance noteworthy inconsistencies and use approaches to trauma and memory grounded in current scientific findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of cross-examination trade-offs and impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: The preamble records extensive commenter evidence both that cross-examination can be critical to assessing credibility (exposing inconsistencies) and that cross-examination can retraumatize victims and reduce reporting; decisions about cross-examination procedures implicate trauma, truth-finding, and due process concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should weigh empirical literature on cross-examination's effects (e.g., on adult and child witnesses, memory accuracy, trauma responses) when designing hearing procedures; training and procedural safeguards can mitigate harms while preserving fact-finding integrity consistent with due process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal evidentiary rules not strictly required in campus proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters and case law (e.g., Flaim v. Med. Coll. of Ohio) note that Federal or State rules of evidence do not apply to college disciplinary proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While traditional courtroom evidentiary rules may not bind campus processes, recipients must still apply their adopted rules equally to both parties and ensure processes are fair, transparent, and consistent with Title IX requirements.
